approaches.name: Trochanteric flip osteotomy for acetabular exposure
approaches.corridor: Modified Gibson or Kocher-Langenbeck exposure with a digastric greater-trochanter fragment carrying gluteus medius and vastus lateralis

sources.title: Rationales for the Bernese approaches in acetabular surgery
Use of a trochanteric flip osteotomy improves outcomes in Pipkin IV fractures

procedure_applications.condition: Cranial, anterior, or intra-articular visualization exceeds a standard posterior exposure

positioning.text: Use lateral positioning when a modified Gibson interval and hip motion are needed; maintain knee flexion near 90 degrees and avoid prolonged hip flexion to reduce sciatic-nerve tension.

setup.text: Prep the leg freely for flexion, rotation, distraction, and possible figure-four surgical dislocation; plan trochanter reattachment before making the osteotomy.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the iliac crest, greater trochanter, femoral shaft, and course of the posterior border of gluteus medius.

incision.text: For the modified Gibson variant, use a straight lateral incision extending roughly 10–15 cm proximal and distal to the greater trochanter, adjusted for habitus and required exposure.

superficial_interval.text: Develop the interval between gluteus maximus and medius proximally and continue distally through the iliotibial tract, preserving gluteus-medius fascia with maximus to protect its vascular supply.

deep_interval.text: Identify the sciatic nerve and anatomic variants, develop the piriformis–gluteus-minimus interval, mobilize minimus from the retroacetabular surface, and preserve the short rotators and retinacular circulation whenever possible.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, gluteal and iliotibial fascia, Gibson or posterior muscular interval, gluteus-minimus plane, digastric trochanteric osteotomy, capsule, and acetabular rim.

structures_encountered.text: Gluteus maximus, medius and minimus, vastus lateralis, piriformis, short external rotators, sciatic nerve, circumflex vascular anastomoses, capsule, labrum, and acetabular rim are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: The sciatic nerve, superior gluteal neurovascular bundle, medial femoral circumflex and retinacular vessels, labrum, femoral-head cartilage, and trochanteric fragment are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Keep the capsulotomy anterior to the lesser trochanter and preserve inferior retinacular tissues; an overly thick osteotomy or posterior stripping can injure femoral-head perfusion.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid sustained sciatic-nerve traction, protect gluteus minimus during retraction, and release anomalous piriformis anatomy when necessary rather than tensioning a divided nerve variant.

exposure.text: Adds cranial and anterior retroacetabular and supra-acetabular visualization to a posterior or Gibson exposure; surgical dislocation can provide direct circumferential articular assessment.

limitations.text: This extensile adjunct adds osteotomy fixation, abductor morbidity, and nonunion risk and may still require hip relocation for safe implant insertion.

extensions.text: A Z-shaped capsulotomy and controlled figure-four surgical dislocation may be added for full articular access; preserve the capsular pedicle of posterior-wall fragments.

indications.text: Use when complex posterior, transverse, T-type, femoral-head, or combined injuries require cranial, anterior, or direct intra-articular visualization unavailable through the base exposure.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid routine use when a standard exposure provides adequate reduction and fixation, or when abductor dysfunction, poor trochanteric bone, or local soft-tissue compromise makes osteotomy healing unreliable.

implant_implications.text: Predrill the trochanter when helpful and plan reattachment with two or three lag screws sized to bone quality; implant paths must not compromise later acetabular fixation.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use standard acetabular views to confirm column and wall reduction, screw safety, congruity after relocation, and trochanteric reduction and fixation.

closure.text: Loosely repair capsule, anatomically reduce and compress the trochanter, restore vastus-lateralis fascia and released rotators, and close gluteal fascia and iliotibial tract in layers.

complications.text: Complications include sciatic or superior-gluteal injury, femoral-head osteonecrosis, trochanteric nonunion or migration, abductor weakness, heterotopic ossification, cartilage injury, and infection.

bailouts.text: If safe articular access requires excessive nerve or vascular tension, relocate the hip, reassess the interval, and use an alternative or sequential approach rather than enlarging dissection blindly.

questions.question: Which two muscle attachments remain on a digastric trochanteric fragment?
questions.answer: Gluteus medius proximally and vastus lateralis distally.

questions.question: What positioning reduces sciatic-nerve tension during this exposure?
questions.answer: Knee flexion near 90 degrees with the hip kept extended when possible.

questions.question: What additional visualization does the osteotomy provide?
questions.answer: Cranial and anterior acetabular exposure, with complete articular visualization if surgical dislocation is added.
